hand.title: Yousry et al. (1997), Localization of the motor hand area to a knob on the precentral gyrus
hand.type: primary human fMRI and cadaver anatomy

fef.title: Lobel et al. (2001), Localization of human frontal eye fields

s1larynx.title: Miyaji et al. (2014), Neuromagnetic detection of the laryngeal area: sensory-evoked fields to air-puff stimulation

m1larynx.title: Dichter et al. (2018), The control of vocal pitch in human laryngeal motor cortex
m1larynx.type: primary human intracranial recording and stimulation

s2.title: Ruben et al. (2001), Somatotopic organization of human secondary somatosensory cortex
s2.supportSummary: Finger/hallux stimulation in eight participants supported contralateral and ipsilateral S2 organization; S2 topography was less fine grained than S1. Current bilateral opercular wording is appropriate.

rsc.title: Takahashi et al. (1997), Pure topographic disorientation due to right retrosplenial lesion
rsc.supportSummary: Three hemorrhagic lesions involved right retrosplenial and adjacent medial parietal tissue. Supports possible navigation impairment; does not isolate a universal right-only cortical parcel syndrome.

cc.title: Hofer and Frahm (2006), Topography of the human corpus callosum revisited

recordAssessments.name: Caudate nucleus, head
recordAssessments.decision: retain scientific prose with stated limitations
recordAssessments.assessment: Retain anterior bulge in frontal-horn wall medial to anterior capsule. Associative/oculomotor/motivational loops overlap; abulia/language signs vary by side and extent. Motor deficit is appropriately tied to adjacent capsule; Huntington atrophy includes putamen.

scientificOriginal.name: Caudate nucleus, head
scientificOriginal.function: The enlarged anterior caudate forms a bulge along the lateral wall of the frontal horn, medial to the anterior limb of the internal capsule. It participates in associative, oculomotor and motivational corticostriatal loops; functional territories overlap rather than dividing cleanly at the head/body boundary.

afferent: Prefrontal, cingulate and other corticostriatal glutamatergic inputs
Nigrostriatal dopamine and intralaminar thalamic inputs
efferent: GABAergic projections to pallidal segments and substantia nigra pars reticulata
Outputs organized in direct/indirect and additional recurrent basal-ganglia networks

scientificOriginal.bloodSupply: Recurrent artery of Heubner/other ACA perforators and MCA lenticulostriate branches, with variable territories.

clinical.findings: Can produce abulia, executive/behavioral changes or language/attention deficits according to side and associated injury; a motor deficit often reflects adjacent capsule involvement.
Striatal degeneration, including caudate and putamen, contributes to motor, cognitive and psychiatric manifestations; caudate atrophy can enlarge the frontal horns.
clinical.note: Degenerative, not a focal vascular syndrome.

recordAssessments.name: Putamen
recordAssessments.decision: retain scientific prose with stated limitations
recordAssessments.assessment: Retain lateral lentiform and capsule/claustrum/insula relations. Classical GABAergic direct/indirect outputs are qualified by recurrent circuitry. Putaminal hemorrhage weakness is attributed to capsule; Parkinson degeneration is appropriately localized to SNc.

scientificOriginal.name: Putamen
scientificOriginal.function: The putamen is the lateral component of the lentiform nucleus and a major sensorimotor striatal input region. It lies lateral to pallidum, separated from the insula by external capsule, claustrum and extreme capsule. Its motor, associative and limbic territories overlap within corticostriatal networks.

afferent: Motor/premotor/somatosensory corticostriatal inputs
SNc dopaminergic and centromedian-parafascicular thalamic inputs
efferent: GABAergic projections to GPi/SNr and GPe in the classical direct/indirect pathways
Other recurrent striatal/basal-ganglia network connections

scientificOriginal.bloodSupply: Mainly MCA lenticulostriate branches, with variable anterior choroidal/ACA contributions.

clinical.findings: May cause contralateral weakness/sensory loss through adjacent capsule injury, with gaze or consciousness changes when extensive.
Loss of nigrostriatal dopamine alters striatal and wider basal-ganglia activity; the primary degenerating population is in SNc.
clinical.note: Common DBS targets are STN or GPi; this record is not a treatment recommendation.

recordAssessments.decision: retain scientific prose with stated limitations

scientificOriginal.name: Globus pallidus, external segment
scientificOriginal.function: GPe is the lateral pallidal segment, between putamen and GPi, separated by medullary laminae. It provides inhibitory projections to STN and other basal-ganglia targets and receives substantial excitatory STN input. The indirect-pathway teaching model captures only part of its recurrent circuitry.

afferent: GABAergic striatopallidal input
Glutamatergic STN input and recurrent pallidal connections
efferent: GABAergic projections to STN, GPi/SNr and striatal targets, varying by cell population

scientificOriginal.bloodSupply: MCA lenticulostriate and anterior choroidal supply, with variability.

clinical.findings: Focal or bilateral pallidal damage can accompany movement disorders, but dystonia is not predicted reliably by a simple GPe-STN firing-rate chain.
Carbon monoxide and other hypoxic/toxic exposures can involve both pallidal segments and wider brain networks; patterns vary.
clinical.note: Avoid treating all toxins as selective GPe lesions.

scientificOriginal.name: Globus pallidus, internal segment
scientificOriginal.function: GPi is the medial pallidal segment next to the internal capsule and is a major GABAergic basal-ganglia output nucleus alongside SNr. Pallidothalamic axons travel via ansa lenticularis/lenticular fasciculus into the thalamic fasciculus; outputs also reach brainstem targets. Firing patterns and network timing are as relevant as mean rate.

afferent: Direct striatal inhibitory and STN excitatory input
GPe and other modulatory/recurrent basal-ganglia inputs
efferent: Motor/association thalamus through pallidothalamic pathways
Brainstem targets including pedunculopontine/reticular regions

clinical.findings: Pallidal injury can produce dystonia, parkinsonism or hyperkinetic syndromes depending on extent and network effects.

scientificOriginal.name: Ventral striatum
scientificOriginal.function: The ventral striatum includes nucleus accumbens and ventromedial caudate/putamen territories near the basal forebrain. It integrates cortical and limbic information with dopaminergic modulation in motivation, reinforcement learning and action selection. It overlaps the accumbens record rather than representing a separate encapsulated nucleus.

efferent: Ventral pallidum and other basal-ganglia targets

scientificOriginal.name: CN I Olfactory nerve
scientificOriginal.function: CN I consists of primary olfactory receptor-neuron axons (olfactory fila) from the superior nasal neuroepithelium to the bulb. Mitral/tufted cells then project in the CNS olfactory tract to primary olfactory regions without a compulsory initial thalamic relay. Olfaction contributes to flavor and emotional/memory networks, but it is distinct from gustatory taste.

efferent: First synapse in olfactory-bulb glomeruli on mitral/tufted cells
Bulb output continues in olfactory tract to piriform/periamygdaloid and other olfactory regions; higher processing includes orbitofrontal/MD pathways

scientificOriginal.bloodSupply: Nasal mucosa is supplied by ethmoidal and other nasal arteries; bulb/tract receive small ACA/carotid-system branches. Segment-specific territory is not mapped here.

A large anterior cranial-fossa lesion can cause ipsilateral optic atrophy and contralateral papilledema, sometimes with anosmia; the full pattern is uncommon.

scientificOriginal.name: CN II Optic nerve
scientificOriginal.function: CN II conveys retinal ganglion-cell output from one eye through the optic canal to the chiasm. The optic nerve is a CNS tract by development and myelination, conventionally named a cranial nerve. Its retinal axons contribute to visual, pupillary and circadian pathways after their central continuation.

afferent: Retinal ganglion-cell axons from the ipsilateral eye; retinal circuitry has already processed the input
efferent: Continuation through chiasm into optic tracts

scientificOriginal.name: Hippocampus
scientificOriginal.function: The hippocampal formation curves along the medial floor of the temporal horn and includes hippocampus proper, dentate gyrus and subiculum in common usage. The whole structure is not a single nucleus.

retainedLimitations.detail: No independent registered patient/standard-atlas comparison validates custom origin3d, size3d, level intersections, patches, ribbon segmentation, waypoint trajectories or microscopic field boundaries. Book figures support relative gross anatomy, not numerical coordinate or exact boundary replacements.

Gyri, sulci, Brodmann areas, functional fMRI parcels and individual cortical networks are not interchangeable. New concepts lacking independent segmentation are useful searchable teaching entries; a whole-gyrus name must not silently assert one deterministic function.

Eight-segment mirrored strips simplify overlapping, interleaved and multiple maps. Apparent proximity to a host mesh is not fMRI validation. Oral/laryngeal placement, exact order, size and bilateral symmetry are especially uncertain; human S1 larynx evidence prevents deletion solely because a textbook homunculus omits it. Dorsal human laryngeal motor evidence prevents treating one inferior patch as the complete laryngeal cortex.

retainedLimitations.decision: retain broad circuit teaching with species limitations
retainedLimitations.scope: CA fields, entorhinal, dentate, accumbens, ventral pallidum and GPe
retainedLimitations.detail: Cell-type, laminar and subregional wiring relies substantially on rodent/nonhuman-primate experiments. Current explicit animal labels and preferential rather than exclusive projections should remain. These are not complete individually measured human tract diagrams.

Arterial branches and territories vary and overlap. Gross ACA/MCA/PCA/Heubner/anterior-choroidal assignments do not validate microvascular CA/dentate boundaries or fixed cortical patch supply. No deterministic watershed replacements are proposed.

A displayed coordinate or structural label does not diagnose a syndrome. Current laterality and adjacent-injury explanations are appropriately qualified: capsule injury explains many striatal motor signs; dominant networks govern aphasia; isolated subfield syndromes generally are not established.

Adult human neurogenesis has supporting molecular/postmortem evidence including a real 2026 citation, while measured abundance, rate and functional impact remain method-dependent. Older conflicting evidence is not erased; textbook second edition cannot itself validate 2026 claims.

Basal ganglia can be used as a broad traditional topographic subdivision. Current prose correctly places claustrum outside the standard motor basal-ganglia circuit and qualifies consciousness/attention claims. Keep the explicit distinction rather than inventing a replacement functional group.

Human tractography supports broad frontal/sensorimotor/posterior callosal distributions, with variable borders and disagreement with older primate-based partitions. No fixed coordinate or exclusive regional fiber border is asserted.
